name: Maurya Empire
summary: The first empire to unite most of the Indian subcontinent. Emperor Ashoka turned to Buddhism after the bloody Kalinga war.

knownFor.label: Edicts of Ashoka
knownFor.note: Rock and pillar inscriptions promoting dhamma (moral conduct).

knownFor.label: Arthashastra
knownFor.note: A treatise on statecraft linked to Chanakya.

location.value: Most of the Indian subcontinent, ruled from Pataliputra (near modern Patna). At its greatest extent under Ashoka it reached from Afghanistan to Bengal and south into the Deccan.

terrain.value: The Ganges plain as the core, plus the Indus region, the Deccan and the Himalayan foothills.

climate.value: Monsoon climate, with rains from June to September.

resources.value: Fertile Ganges farmland, forests, elephants and iron.

disasters.value: Not documented in the sources checked.

population.value: About 15–30 million in the 3rd century BCE (Wikipedia infobox).

urbanisation.value: Pataliputra was one of the largest cities in the world, described by the Greek envoy Megasthenes.

disease.value: Not documented in the sources checked.

migration.value: After the Kalinga war, large numbers of captives were deported, according to Ashoka’s edicts.

economicBase.value: Agriculture, much of it on state-owned land, plus trade, crafts and mining.

tradeRoutes.value: The Uttarapath (northern highway) and river and sea trade, with contacts with the Hellenistic world.

wealth.value: No estimate is possible; Greek visitors such as Megasthenes described a rich capital at Pataliputra.

moneyAndTax.value: Punch-marked silver karshapana coins. Land taxes and state monopolies (described in the Arthashastra, possibly a later compilation).

inequality.value: Caste consolidated in the Ganges plain. A powerful state elite.

governmentType.value: A centralised monarchy with an emperor, princely governors, a council of ministers, spies and city boards.

keyRulers.value: Chandragupta Maurya (c. 321–298 BCE, founder, advised by Chanakya). Bindusara (298–272). Ashoka the Great (268–232 BCE). Brihadratha (last, killed 185 BCE).

succession.value: Hereditary, but disputed: a struggle of about four years came before Ashoka’s accession.

institutions.value: Ashoka’s rock and pillar edicts set out his “dhamma” (moral law), with welfare measures and animal protection.

stability.value: Revolts in Taxila and Ujjain under Bindusara and Ashoka were suppressed.

eliteConflict.value: Succession struggles. The last emperor was assassinated by his general Pushyamitra Shunga.

armyAndTech.value: Large armies with infantry, cavalry, chariots and war elephants. Greek sources give very large numbers.

majorWars.value: Conquest of the Nanda Empire (c. 321 BCE). War with Seleucus I (about 303 BCE, after which Seleucus ceded the northwest for 500 elephants). The Kalinga War (c. 261 BCE).

territoryChange.value: The first empire to unify most of the subcontinent. It shrank after Ashoka’s death.

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals: the Nandas, the Seleucid Empire (later diplomatic partner) and Kalinga. The Tamil kingdoms in the far south stayed independent.

inventions.value: Polished stone pillars (e.g. the Lion Capital of Sarnath, now India’s national emblem), stupas and rock-cut caves.

scienceEducation.value: Brahmi script (in Ashoka’s edicts), the earliest deciphered writing in India.

openness.value: Diplomatic links with Hellenistic kings. Ashoka sent Buddhist missions abroad.

religion.value: Brahmanism, Jainism (Chandragupta reportedly became a Jain monk), Buddhism (promoted by Ashoka) and the Ajivikas.

languageWriting.value: Magadhi Prakrit and other Prakrits, and likely Sanskrit for literature. Brahmi and Kharosthi scripts.

artsArchitecture.value: Ashoka’s pillars, the Great Stupa at Sanchi (begun under Ashoka) and the Barabar caves.

socialStructure.value: A varna (caste) hierarchy, more rigid in the Ganges plain. Slaves and labourers existed.

sharedIdentity.value: Ashoka’s dhamma promoted a moral community across a diverse empire.

neighbours.value: The Seleucid Empire, Greco-Bactria, Kalinga, the Tamil kingdoms (Cholas, Pandyas, Cheras) and Sri Lanka.

ideasReligions.value: Ashoka sent Buddhist missionaries to Sri Lanka and beyond, beginning Buddhism’s spread across Asia.

colonisation.value: Conquered most of India. Its rule over conquered peoples is recorded in its own edicts.

riseSignals.value: Chandragupta (with Chanakya) overthrew the Nandas and filled the vacuum left by Alexander’s retreat from the northwest.

peakPeriod.value: The reign of Ashoka (about 268–232 BCE), whose edicts were carved across the empire.

declineSignals.value: Weak successors, the empire dividing, regional independence, a top-heavy administration, and Greco-Bactrian invasions. Blaming Ashoka’s pacifism is described by Romila Thapar as “grossly exaggerated”.

outcome.value: Overthrow. Pushyamitra Shunga killed the last emperor Brihadratha (185 BCE) and founded the Shunga Empire.

sources.value: Ashoka’s edicts, Megasthenes (via later Greek writers), the Arthashastra, Buddhist and Jain texts, and archaeology. Checked against Wikipedia on 6 Nov 2026. See also Thapar (2002).

overallCertainty.value: Moderate. Dates vary (founding c. 322–320 BCE; Ashoka’s reign 272 or 268–232). The Arthashastra’s dating and Chandragupta’s religion are debated.
